tests.title: iTEP Practice Test III
instructions: This exam follows an iTEP-style format with five sections.
Complete sections in order and manage your time carefully.
Listening is forward-only and each audio can be played once.
Speaking allows one recording per task.

questions.prompt: There ____ a lot of information on that website about local events.
questions.explanation: 'Information' is an uncountable noun and takes the singular verb 'is'.

questions.prompt: My teacher speaks very clearly. I always understand ____.
questions.explanation: After a verb, use an object pronoun ('her'), not a subject pronoun ('she').

questions.prompt: She ____ that film three times already; she knows every line.
questions.explanation: Present perfect (have/has + past participle) expresses experience up to now.

questions.prompt: This road is ____ the highway, so the drive takes longer.
questions.explanation: One-syllable adjectives form comparatives with '-er than': 'narrower than'.

questions.prompt: Look at those clouds — it ____ rain any minute now.
questions.explanation: 'Going to' expresses a prediction based on present evidence (the clouds we can see).

questions.prompt: He ____ in this apartment for six years and has no plans to move.
questions.explanation: Present perfect continuous (has/have been + -ing) stresses the duration of an action continuing to now.

questions.prompt: You ____ wear a seatbelt at all times; it is required by law.
questions.explanation: 'Must' expresses a strong obligation or legal requirement; 'should' is weaker and advisory.

questions.prompt: ____ of the candidates gave a convincing speech, so voters remained undecided.
questions.explanation: 'Neither' is used for two items with a negative meaning without the word 'not'.

questions.prompt: I wish I ____ more time to read for pleasure during the semester.
questions.explanation: After 'wish', use the past simple to express an unreal or regretted present situation.

questions.prompt: It was the project manager ____ identified the error before the deadline.
questions.explanation: In a cleft sentence referring to a person, use 'who' (or 'that') after 'it was'.

questions.prompt: She ____ her apartment repainted before the tenants moved in.
questions.explanation: Causative 'have' (have + object + past participle) means to arrange for someone else to do something.

questions.prompt: ____ the authorities been notified sooner, the damage could have been minimized.
questions.explanation: Inverted third conditional: 'Had + subject + past participle' replaces 'If + subject + had + past participle'.

questions.prompt: ____ carefully through the data, the analyst discovered a previously overlooked pattern.
questions.explanation: A perfect participle clause ('Having worked') shows an action completed before the main verb.

questions.prompt: Yesterday, she is walking to school when she found a lost dog.
questions.explanation: For a past action at a specific time, use past simple or past continuous: 'was walking'.

questions.prompt: He is studying to be a engineer at the local technical college.
questions.explanation: 'Engineer' begins with a vowel sound, so the correct article is 'an', not 'a'.

questions.prompt: The company decided investing in renewable energy sources last quarter.
questions.explanation: 'Decide' is followed by an infinitive, not a gerund: 'decided to invest'.

questions.prompt: The number of students enrolled in online courses have increased significantly.
questions.explanation: 'The number of' takes a singular verb: 'has increased', not 'have increased'.

questions.prompt: She has been interested on marine biology since she was a teenager.
questions.explanation: The correct collocation is 'interested in', not 'interested on'.

questions.prompt: Running through the park, the rain suddenly began to fall heavily.
questions.explanation: The participial phrase 'Running through the park' must refer to the subject of the main clause; the rain cannot run. Rewrite: 'Running through the park, she was caught in the heavy rain.'

questions.prompt: The new policy will have a major affect on how employees submit their timesheets.
questions.explanation: 'Affect' is a verb; the noun is 'effect'. The sentence requires 'a major effect on'.

questions.prompt: The report, that was released yesterday, confirms the earlier predictions.
questions.explanation: A non-restrictive relative clause describing a specific noun uses 'which', not 'that': 'which was released yesterday'.

questions.prompt: The package was suppose to arrive on Tuesday but never came.
questions.explanation: The passive requires the past participle: 'was supposed to'.

questions.prompt: If she had practiced more consistently, she would be a professional musician now.
questions.explanation: This sentence is grammatically correct — it is a mixed conditional: past perfect in the if-clause (past) and 'would + base form' in the result (present).
questions.note: This question tests recognition of correct grammar; -1 indicates no error.

questions.prompt: The committee insists that every delegate signs the agreement before the vote.
questions.explanation: After verbs of insistence, the subjunctive requires the base form: 'that every delegate sign'.

questions.prompt: She finished the marathon faster than I did, although I trained harder than she.
questions.explanation: After a comparative clause with an auxiliary, include the auxiliary: 'than she did', not 'than she'.

items.transcript: Conversation one. Woman: Have you tried the new café near the campus library? Man: Not yet. Is it any good? Woman: The coffee is great and they have free Wi-Fi, but it gets really crowded after noon. Man: Good to know — I will go early tomorrow.

questions.prompt: What problem does the woman mention about the café?
options: It becomes very crowded after noon
It is too far from campus
questions.explanation: The woman says the café gets really crowded after noon.

items.transcript: Conversation two. Man: Excuse me, I left my umbrella on the bus this morning. Can you help me? Agent: Of course. What does it look like? Man: It is dark blue with a wooden handle. Agent: Let me check our lost and found. Please fill out this form and we will call you if it turns up.

questions.prompt: What does the agent ask the man to do?
questions.explanation: The agent asks the man to fill out a form so they can contact him if the umbrella is found.

items.transcript: Conversation three. Woman A: I am so nervous about the presentation tomorrow. Woman B: Have you rehearsed it yet? Woman A: Twice, but I keep forgetting the third slide. Woman B: Try recording yourself — it really helps to hear where you pause too long.

questions.prompt: What advice does Woman B give?
options: Practice in front of a mirror
Ask a friend to present instead
questions.explanation: Woman B suggests recording herself to hear where she pauses too long.

items.transcript: Conversation four. Manager: We need to finish the quarterly report by Thursday. Can you take the data analysis part? Employee: I can, but I have a client call Thursday morning. Would Wednesday afternoon work for a draft? Manager: That works. Just send it to me before five.

questions.prompt: When does the employee agree to send the draft?
questions.explanation: The employee proposes Wednesday afternoon and the manager agrees, asking for it before five.

items.transcript: Long conversation. Student A: Have you registered for Professor Kim's research methods course next semester? Student B: Not yet. I heard it has a lot of reading. Student A: It does, but she says the final project is worth fifty percent of the grade. Student B: That is actually better than a written exam. Student A: Agreed. The project is on a topic of your choice, which helps. Student B: I am thinking of studying social media use among university students. Student A: That sounds great. We could even collaborate if our topics overlap. Student B: Let us check with Professor Kim first to see if group projects are allowed. Student A: Good idea. Her office hours are Tuesday from two to four.

questions.prompt: What are the students mainly discussing?
options: A current assignment they need to finish
A course they are considering for next semester
questions.explanation: The students discuss whether to register for Professor Kim's research methods course next semester.

questions.prompt: How much of the course grade does the final project represent?
questions.explanation: Student A says the final project is worth fifty percent of the grade.

questions.prompt: What topic is Student B interested in studying?
options: Social media use among university students
questions.explanation: Student B says they are thinking of studying social media use among university students.

questions.prompt: What will the students most likely do next?
options: Ask Professor Kim about collaborating on a project
Submit their individual project topics online
questions.explanation: They agree to check with Professor Kim first to see if group projects are allowed.

items.transcript: Lecture. Professor: Good morning, everyone. Today we are going to look at the concept of urban heat islands. An urban heat island occurs when a city or metropolitan area is significantly warmer than its surrounding rural areas. This temperature difference is primarily caused by human activities and the physical properties of urban materials. Surfaces like concrete, asphalt, and rooftops absorb heat from the sun during the day and release it slowly at night, whereas vegetation in rural areas reflects more sunlight and provides natural cooling through evapotranspiration. The consequences of urban heat islands include increased energy consumption, particularly for air conditioning, higher levels of air pollution, and negative health effects, especially for elderly residents and those with respiratory conditions. Urban planners have proposed several mitigation strategies, such as expanding green spaces, planting trees along streets, and installing reflective or green roofs on buildings. Research indicates that increasing urban tree coverage by even ten percent can meaningfully reduce local temperatures.

questions.prompt: What is the lecture primarily about?
options: The benefits of moving populations to rural areas
Why cities are warmer than surrounding rural areas and how to address this
New regulations for building construction in cities
The history of urban planning in the twentieth century
questions.explanation: The professor explains urban heat islands, their causes, effects, and mitigation strategies.

questions.prompt: The word 'evapotranspiration' in the lecture refers to:
options: The reflection of sunlight off glass buildings
A natural process that releases moisture and cools the air
A form of urban pollution caused by vehicles
The absorption of heat by dark-colored surfaces
questions.explanation: The professor uses it to describe how vegetation provides natural cooling, implying the release of moisture that lowers temperatures.

questions.prompt: Why do urban surfaces retain more heat than rural areas at night?
options: Cities produce more pollution that traps heat
Urban materials like concrete absorb heat during the day and release it slowly
Buildings block the wind, preventing natural cooling
Rural areas have more rivers that cool the surrounding land
questions.explanation: The professor states that concrete, asphalt, and rooftops absorb heat during the day and release it slowly at night.

questions.prompt: According to the professor, which groups are most negatively affected by urban heat islands?
options: Elderly residents and those with respiratory conditions
questions.explanation: The professor specifically mentions elderly residents and people with respiratory conditions as the most vulnerable.

questions.prompt: What does the professor imply about increasing tree coverage in cities?
options: It is too expensive for most cities to implement
Even a modest increase can have a meaningful impact on local temperatures
It is only effective in cities with very low pollution levels
Trees require too much water to be practical in urban settings
questions.explanation: The professor states that increasing tree coverage by just ten percent can meaningfully reduce local temperatures.

questions.prompt: What can be inferred about green roofs based on the lecture?
options: They are required by law in most cities
They are one potential strategy to help reduce urban heat
They are only suitable for residential buildings
They have been proven ineffective in recent studies
questions.explanation: Green roofs are mentioned among mitigation strategies proposed by urban planners.

passages.title: The Rise of Slow Travel
passages.text:
In recent years, a growing number of travelers have begun to reject fast-paced itineraries in favor of a more deliberate approach known as slow travel. Rather than rushing from city to city in order to check destinations off a list, slow travelers choose to spend extended periods in a single location, immersing themselves in local culture, forming connections with residents, and developing a deeper understanding of the places they visit.

The slow travel movement draws on principles similar to those of the slow food movement, which advocates for quality and mindfulness over speed and convenience. Proponents argue that spending a week or a month in one place — cooking local ingredients, using public transportation, and attending neighborhood events — produces a far richer experience than a conventional two-week tour of ten countries.

Slow travel also tends to be more environmentally sustainable. Fewer flights means a lower carbon footprint, and staying in locally owned accommodations rather than international hotel chains keeps money circulating within the local economy. Despite its advantages, slow travel requires resources that not everyone has: time, flexibility, and often a location-independent income.

questions.prompt: What is the passage mainly about?
options: How to find cheap airline tickets for long trips
A travel philosophy that prioritizes depth over speed
The environmental damage caused by tourism
A comparison of popular tourist destinations
questions.explanation: The passage describes the slow travel movement and its principles, benefits, and limitations.

questions.prompt: What movement is slow travel compared to in the passage?
questions.explanation: The passage draws a direct comparison between slow travel and the slow food movement.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, how does slow travel benefit local economies?
options: By encouraging travelers to visit multiple countries
By keeping money in locally owned businesses rather than international chains
By reducing the need for public transportation infrastructure
By promoting the construction of new hotels in remote areas
questions.explanation: The passage states that staying in locally owned accommodations keeps money circulating within the local economy.

questions.prompt: The word 'deliberate' in the first paragraph is closest in meaning to:
questions.explanation: 'Deliberate' means done with intention and care; here it contrasts with the rushed pace of conventional tourism.

questions.prompt: What does the passage imply about who can most easily adopt slow travel?
options: People who are retired or who can work remotely
Business travelers with corporate expense accounts
Anyone willing to reduce their spending on accommodation
questions.explanation: The passage notes that slow travel requires time, flexibility, and often a location-independent income — traits more common among remote workers or retirees.

passages.title: The Neuroscience of Music
passages.text:
Music is one of the most complex stimuli the human brain processes. Unlike language or visual perception, music activates an unusually broad network of brain regions simultaneously, including areas responsible for auditory processing, memory, emotion, and movement. Neuroscientists have used brain imaging techniques such as fMRI to map these responses, revealing that the brain does not simply hear music passively but actively predicts and responds to it in real time. [A]

One of the most studied phenomena is the 'chills' response — the physical sensation of goosebumps or shivers that some people experience when listening to emotionally powerful music. Research suggests that this response involves the release of dopamine, the brain's reward chemical, in the nucleus accumbens, a region also associated with the pleasures of food and social bonding. Interestingly, not everyone experiences this response, and those who do tend to score higher on measures of openness to experience. [B]

Music also has well-documented effects on memory and mood. It is widely used in therapeutic contexts for patients with Alzheimer's disease, many of whom can remember song lyrics even when other forms of memory have significantly deteriorated. [C] Music-based interventions have been shown to reduce anxiety in hospital settings and improve motor coordination in patients undergoing rehabilitation after a stroke.

Despite the growing body of research, much remains unknown about why music affects humans as profoundly as it does. [D] Some researchers propose that music's emotional power derives from its structural parallels with human speech — specifically, its use of rhythm, pitch, and timing to convey meaning and intention.

questions.prompt: Which statement best summarizes the passage?
options: Music is processed only in the auditory cortex and has little effect on emotion
The brain responds to music across multiple regions, and music has measurable effects on memory, emotion, and health
The main benefit of music is in improving motor skills after illness
Scientists have fully explained why music triggers emotional responses in humans
questions.explanation: The passage covers how music activates multiple brain regions and has documented effects on emotion, memory, and therapeutic outcomes.

questions.prompt: What chemical is associated with the 'chills' response to music?
questions.explanation: The passage states the chills response involves the release of dopamine in the nucleus accumbens.

questions.prompt: What does the passage say about people who experience the 'chills' response to music?
options: They are more likely to be professional musicians
They tend to score higher on measures of openness to experience
They process music in a different region of the brain
They are less likely to benefit from music therapy
questions.explanation: The passage states those who experience the chills tend to score higher on openness to experience.

questions.prompt: What does the passage imply about music and Alzheimer's disease?
options: Music can fully restore long-term memory in Alzheimer's patients
Music memory may be more resistant to deterioration than other forms of memory
Music therapy has been rejected as ineffective in medical settings
Patients can only respond to music if they were musicians before diagnosis
questions.explanation: The passage says Alzheimer's patients can remember song lyrics even when other memory has deteriorated, implying music memory is relatively preserved.

questions.prompt: The word 'profoundly' in the final paragraph is closest in meaning to:
questions.explanation: 'Profoundly' means deeply or to a great degree; the passage uses it to describe how strongly music affects humans.

questions.prompt: Where would this sentence most logically appear in the passage? 'This predictive processing helps explain why unexpected notes or harmonies can feel either thrilling or jarring.'
questions.explanation: Position [A] follows the statement that the brain actively predicts and responds to music; the inserted sentence directly extends this idea by explaining an effect of those predictions.

prompts.prompt: Your colleague is starting at your company next week and will be working in your department. Write a short note welcoming them, mentioning one useful tip about the team and suggesting a day you could meet for lunch.

Some people argue that social media has had an overall positive effect on society by helping people stay connected and share information freely. Others believe it has caused more harm than good by spreading misinformation and damaging mental health. In your opinion, has social media been a positive or negative development for society? Support your answer with specific reasons and examples.
Describe a goal you have set for yourself in the next year. What is the goal, what steps are you taking to achieve it, and what challenges do you expect to face? Give specific details and examples.

Some people believe that learning a foreign language should be mandatory for all students from an early age, arguing that it improves cognitive development and opens professional opportunities. Others contend that limited school time is better spent on core subjects like mathematics and science. Which view do you support, and why? Consider both perspectives in your response.
